## Session Pivot

The object has acquired consistency precisely where the Other cannot know desire completely. The next session must therefore push the relation between demand, desire, and lack further, and it does so by expanding the topological repertoire beyond the torus toward one-sided surfaces and by sharpening the privileged `D + d` circuit.

# Session 15 - 28 March 1962

**Printed source pages:** 200-218

## Opening Problem

Lacan resumes with the torus as a general topological support for the seminar. He now emphasizes that topology concerns properties preserved through deformation. The familiar ring shape is therefore only one presentation of the torus. This opens the way to compare it with other surfaces, especially the cross-cap or mitre and the one-sided property illustrated by a twisted strip.

## Argument Reconstruction

### From the torus to one-sided surfaces

Lacan describes topology as a "rubber geometry" in which stretching and deformation do not destroy the relevant relations. A torus can be represented as a sphere with a handle. More complicated orientable closed surfaces can be approached by adding handles. But Lacan also introduces a different kind of surface, designated in English as the "cross-cap" and in the French discussion by "mitre."

The key property that interests him is a continuity by which what ordinary intuition calls the outside can pass into what it calls the inside. He illustrates this one-sidedness with a strip of paper given a half-twist and glued to itself. The strip demonstrates the property clearly, but the source does not simply identify every one-sided strip with the full cross-cap construction.

This is a major conceptual step. Inside/outside is no longer treated as a primitive distinction to which psychic meanings are later attached. A surface can make the distinction dependent on a path and a cut.

### Demand as repeated circuit

Returning to the torus, Lacan reiterates that the repeated turns around the generating dimension can represent successive demands. These turns are "the same" only through the unary operation that counts them. Their repetition produces the other circularity associated with desire.

Desire is thus not another demand added to the list. It is metonymically generated across the succession of demands and becomes legible through a circuit that the subject does not count as one more item of the series.

### The privileged combined circuit `D + d`

Lacan identifies a special closed curve that does two things at once. It goes around the thickness of the torus while also taking in the central hole. He represents this privileged circuit as the addition of the two basic circularities, `D + d`.

The importance of the construction is that demand and desire are neither identical nor cleanly separable. A single path can traverse both dimensions. Moreover, more than one `D + d` curve can be drawn on the same torus without coincidence. This supports an "either...or" relation and prevents the privileged circuit from becoming a new image of total unity.

The source's diagrams explore how such circles occupy sectors of the toroidal surface and how a cutting plane can be tangent to the torus so as to pick out the exceptional circuit. The geometry is used to make the logical relation visible, not to prove a theorem independent of the analytic problem.

### Aphanisis, Jones, and the object of anxiety

The session then returns to psychoanalytic disputes over sexuality, especially Ernest Jones's theory of female sexuality and *aphanisis*. Jones defines a fundamental fear of the disappearance of sexual capacity or desire. Lacan argues that the analytic problem cannot be located simply in the empirical disappearance of desire.

What produces anxiety is bound to the hidden object, to the truth of desire, and to the desire of the Other. The subject can choose between an object and the persistence of desire only because both are already structured by the signifier. Lacan also touches on female homosexuality and repression in this context, using the clinical debates to show that a naturalized developmental account misses the formal place of the phallus.

### Why the phallus occupies a privileged place

The phallus returns because it is the signifying instrument around which the void in demand is organized. It is not simply the penis as a biological organ. Its privilege is connected with measure, lack, and the passage beyond a pleasure-principle model in which satisfaction would terminate the circuit.

Desire persists because no object closes demand. Repetition therefore remains constitutive. The session ends by playing on the domain of *n'être* / *naître*, non-being and being born. The child can occupy the place of what was desired, but the fact of having been desired is structurally different from being the positive completion of parental lack. A desire for a child can be transmitted as blessing, burden, or curse because the child enters a pre-existing signifying field.

## Identification Development

Identification now enters a topological field where the subject cannot be assigned a stable inside and the Other a stable outside. The repeated unary turns of demand generate desire without producing a final unifying trait. The `D + d` circuit shows that the mark of identification can participate simultaneously in demand and desire, while the one-sided surface prepares a stronger model of subject division than any image of a bounded ego.

## Interlocutors and Sources

Ernest Jones is a major interlocutor through *aphanisis* and the debate on female sexuality. Freud remains the background for castration, repression, repetition, and the phallic function. Mathematical topology supplies the torus, handle decomposition, cross-cap/mitre, one-sided strip, and cutting operations. The source's own notes caution against identifying the illustrative one-sided strip with every technical feature of a cross-cap.

## Session Pivot

By the end of March, topology is no longer ancillary. The torus has formalized repetition and the missed circuit; the cross-cap/mitre introduces one-sidedness and a stronger disturbance of inside/outside. The next block develops the subject, desire, fantasy, and castration through increasingly explicit cuts and surface transformations.

# Session 16 - 4 April 1962

**Printed source pages:** 219-230

## Opening Problem

Lacan begins with the ambiguous French word *rapport*, which can mean a report, a relation, or a relationship. The word gives him a way to ask what kind of "relation" can be established to objects such as anxiety and desire. The void at the centre of the torus is his immediate reference. A discourse about desire can only be "not without relation" to the void around which desire is organized.

## Argument Reconstruction

### "Not without" and the void

Lacan returns to the expression *pas sans*, "not without." Access to desire requires that the subject be "not without having it," but what is had cannot simply be specified as a positive object. Human desire repeatedly circles a central hole, a Thing that is approached through its effects rather than possessed directly.

He warns against confusing this structural void with poverty of thought. One cannot respond to a hole in the subject by simply saying less or by treating desire as ineffable. The task is to find formal relations adequate to what the void makes possible.

### Anxiety and the desire of the Other

Lacan now states more explicitly the relation between anxiety and the desire of the Other. The Other is the locus in which the signifying chain unfolds, not another complete subject who can guarantee the law. There is no Other of the Other that would finally certify the truth of the symbolic order. The Other is therefore also the place where the Thing is elided.

The formula "man's desire is the desire of the Other" must not be translated into a sociological proposition that one person simply imitates another person's wishes. Nor is it a relation between two already constituted ego-subjects. The subject is constituted in the very dependence on the field of the Other.

Lacan gives a formal approximation: if one treats the subject's desire and the Other's desire through the imaginary unit, their product does not yield a positive common measure but the lack `-1`. The point is that there can be no contract or commensurability at the level of desire.

### Fantasy as the support of desire

Because desire cannot be realized as a common measure between two persons, fantasy provides its support. Lacan invokes Sade and Freud's *A Child Is Being Beaten* as paradigmatic references. In fantasy, the subject can become the instrument of a desire located elsewhere, beyond the immediately presented object.

This gives a new angle on anxiety. Anxiety appears when the subject encounters the desire of the Other without knowing what object he is for that desire. Lacan's praying-mantis image captures the structure: if the subject were a male mantis facing a larger female and could not see the mark that would tell him what he is for her, he would be exposed to the opaque desire of the Other.

Anxiety is therefore not simply an affect "without an object." The lack of object is on the subject's side: the subject no longer knows what object he may be for the Other. What is missing is the identificatory mark that would locate him in relation to that desire.

### The phallus as mediator

Between demand and desire Lacan places the phallus. The phallic function is what allows desire to be delimited within the field of demand. One may not know the desire of the Other, but one can know the instrument through which desire is mediated.

Castration anxiety accordingly has more than one level. In the woman's relation to the phallus, Lacan follows Freud's account of the phallus as something that can be desired. In the man's case, the organ can serve as support for a phallic function that is not identical with the organ. The passage through castration is therefore a transformation of the relation between the subject, demand, and the signifier of desire.

Lacan insists that the danger for the subject is not simply abandonment by the Other. It is abandonment to demand, because demand is intrinsically interminable. The phallus has to be demanded in order for the field of desire to be established, yet the Other cannot give a final object that would close the demand. Freud's *Analysis Terminable and Interminable* is invoked at this point in connection with unresolved castration anxiety.

### Hysteria and obsession

The hysteric knows in practice that desire is the desire of the Other. She sustains desire by causing or fomenting desire in the Other and can make another person stand proxy in the relation to the desired object. Dora remains the exemplary reference.

The obsessional organizes the relation differently. The paternal demand defines the field and the subject can preserve desire by assigning its fulfilment to the dead man. He may possess and even display the phallus, but desire is displaced into a scene in which the dead Other bears the decisive function.

In both cases anxiety is managed through objects and identifications, but only precariously. Lacan condenses the radical problem in the deliberately crude formula: "the subject demands the phallus and the phallus desires." The point is to show that the subject's relation to the phallus is fundamentally identificatory.

## Identification Development

Identification is now directly tied to anxiety. The subject needs a mark that locates what he is for the desire of the Other. Anxiety appears when that mark fails and the subject can no longer recognize himself as a possible object in the Other's desire. The phallus mediates this relation by supplying a signifying function through which desire can be constituted, but it never restores a complete identity.

# Session 17 - 11 April 1962

**Printed source pages:** 231-254

## Opening Problem

Lacan says he had intended to continue directly with the phallus but will speak of it through an "inverted eight." Hooson's note identifies the surface under discussion as a Möbius-type surface in this sequence. The larger purpose is to refine the topological vocabulary needed to distinguish identity, self-difference, demand, and desire.

## Argument Reconstruction

### Euler circles and the limits of intuitive logic

Lacan begins with Euler circles, historically associated with the diagrammatic representation of classes and syllogisms. A circle on a plane seems to divide an inside from an outside. Inclusion, exclusion, intersection, union, and symmetric difference can then be visualized by overlapping circles.

He is interested in the way modern logic used these simple figures beyond Euler's original pedagogical purpose. The diagrams make relations tangible, but precisely for that reason they can conceal assumptions imported from the plane and from spherical intuition.

The "symmetric difference" of two intersecting circles is especially important. It designates what belongs to one field or the other but not to their intersection. Lacan uses the construction to approach a difference that is internal to repetition rather than a comparison between two independently constituted objects.

### The inverted eight

Lacan asks what happens if the ordinary Euler circle is replaced by an inverted-eight figure in which what seems to be an inner loop continues into the outer loop. The result frustrates the ordinary inside/outside reading. The line cannot be treated simply as two nested circles, because the continuity of the trace makes the apparent interior relation unstable.

He associates this with the problem of an object that cannot simply "take itself up" or reflect itself into itself. In the case of little `a`, what matters is not an object identical with itself but an object whose relation to itself is structured by a difference. The inverted eight becomes a way of representing the self-difference of desire and, more precisely, the conjunction of the object of desire with itself in a relation that does not collapse into identity.

### Three kinds of circles on the torus

Lacan returns to the torus and distinguishes reducible and irreducible loops. A small contractible circle can be tightened to a point. Other circles wind around one or the other fundamental dimension of the torus and cannot be shrunk to zero without cutting the surface.

The cutting consequences differ. Some cuts leave the torus connected even though they open the surface. Cutting along both fundamental directions can flatten the torus into the familiar rectangle with identified edges. A corresponding cut on a sphere, by contrast, separates the surface into two pieces. The difference demonstrates why ordinary planar or spherical intuitions cannot simply be carried over.

### Symmetric difference on a torus

Lacan then draws two intersecting closed curves on the torus and asks whether the Eulerian notions of intersection and symmetric difference still behave as expected. The topology complicates the apparently obvious field of intersection. Regions that look separate in the drawing can turn out to belong to the same continuous surface once the edge identifications are respected.

This is not a recreational puzzle. Lacan wants a formal model in which the same repeated signifying operation can produce a difference that is not reducible to two already separate identities.

### Demand, desire, and the privileged circuit

The repeated circles around the thickness of the torus again serve as demand. Their repetition is at once identical and distinct: each is "the same" demand only insofar as it is another turn. Desire is supported by the other circularity, the circuit generated through the succession of demands.

The privileged circuit combining the two dimensions returns. Lacan compares two demand loops that do not intersect with an inverted-eight path that does. The latter can make the central void of desire tangible within the field of demand itself. This gives the inverted eight its psychoanalytic value beyond its visual novelty.

### Flattened torus and dissymmetry

The torus is cut and represented as a rectangle. Diagonal lines between identified vertices show how loops that appear different on the ring can be structurally related. Lacan is concerned with a problem of orientation: purely as a toroidal surface, the two fundamental types of irreducible loop can be exchanged. But psychoanalytically he needs a dissymmetry between the circuits assigned to demand and those assigned to desire.

He explores several ways to introduce that dissymmetry, including paired or clasped tori and the relation of a torus to an encompassing sphere. A torus can be represented as a handle on a sphere, but an "inner" handle can be deformed into an equivalent torus. The construction demonstrates how difficult it is to derive psychoanalytic asymmetry from the torus alone.

This leads Lacan toward the larger classification of surfaces. The sphere and torus are insufficient. The cross-cap and the possibility of holes must also be introduced. The next stage of the seminar will therefore make non-orientable surfaces central.

## Identification Development

The session gives a topological form to identification as repetition-with-difference. An ordinary Euler circle encourages the image of a self-identical interior. The inverted eight and the torus instead show a mark returning as another occurrence, a loop related to itself through a surface that prevents simple self-inclusion. Identification with the unary trait is thereby aligned with a subject that can only repeat itself by differing from itself.

## Interlocutors and Sources

Euler is central through circle diagrams. De Morgan and later logical uses of class diagrams appear in the historical discussion. Kierkegaard is invoked in relation to the desire of the Other. Descartes and the long cultural history of mathematical instruction are touched on in the opening. The mathematical classification of compact surfaces enters explicitly at the end.

## Session Pivot

The torus has reached an internal limit: by itself it does not supply the asymmetry Lacan needs. The seminar therefore has to introduce the cross-cap and Möbius structure more explicitly. Before that technical development, Session 18 pauses for Piera Aulagnier's clinical intervention on anxiety and identification.

# Session 18 - 2 May 1962

**Printed source pages:** 255-277

## Opening Problem

After the Easter break Lacan gives the floor to Piera Aulagnier. He presents her intervention as a serious attempt to use the distinction between demand and desire in thinking anxiety and identification. The source clearly separates Aulagnier's text from Lacan's later response.

## Argument Reconstruction

### [INTERVENTION - PIERA AULAGNIER] Anxiety and identification

Aulagnier begins from the question whether psychotic anxiety is a distinct type of anxiety. Her proposal is that anxiety, across normal, neurotic, and psychotic structures, responds to a structurally comparable situation of the ego, even though its clinical organization differs.

She treats anxiety as intimately connected with identification. When an identificatory reference collapses, the subject no longer knows where he is situated in relation to the Other. The mirror and the body become especially important in psychosis because the specular organization that ordinarily gives the ego a relatively coherent bodily form can fail to stabilize the subject.

Aulagnier also works through castration, demand, and desire. The phallus is not equated with the penis. The penis can function as an organ, while the phallus functions as a signifier by which the subject may be recognized in the desire of the Other. Castration is thus approached as a passage from a bodily support to a signifying authorization of desire.

Her discussion of orgasm is organized around a temporary coincidence between demand and desire. In sexual jouissance the subject can fleetingly experience himself as recognized by the other as the object of the other's desire while also recognizing the other through the phallic signifier. But this coincidence cannot last. Jouissance is momentary, whereas desire persists; the gap between demand and desire therefore reopens.

Aulagnier then traces the demand/desire distinction into pregenital relations. In the infant's cry, the mother does not merely satisfy a need. By responding she interprets the cry as demand and attributes desire to it. The child enters the field of desire through the unconscious and fantasy of the Other. The maternal interpretation is therefore already a projection that the child must accept, transform, or resist.

The oral object illustrates the point. The breast is at once bodily source of pleasure, external object, gift, and signifier in the relation to the mother's response. Frustration marks the gap between need and desire, while jouissance can reveal something beyond what demand explicitly formulates.

Aulagnier sketches different structural outcomes depending on how identification and castration are negotiated, including neurotic, perverse, and psychotic possibilities. The intervention is not presented by the source as Lacan's own final doctrine.

### Lacan's response: no antinomy of speech and affect

Lacan praises the intervention but says it has gone only halfway. He objects especially when affect is treated as though it belonged to a domain heterogeneous to speech. Human affects, including anxiety and anger, cannot be understood independently of the subject's primary relation to the signifier.

He nevertheless strongly endorses Aulagnier's effective use of demand and desire and singles out her account of sexual jouissance for praise. He agrees that jouissance cannot be understood as fusion or a return to primitive undifferentiation.

### Perverse structure and the phallus

Lacan also takes seriously Aulagnier's formulation of the perverse relation. She proposes the pervert as someone who makes himself object for the jouissance of a phallus whose ownership he does not know, becoming the instrument of the jouissance of a god. Lacan does not endorse every detail but treats the formulation as opening the correct structural field. It makes the definition of the phallus urgent.

### Psychosis, body, and the subject excluded by the signifier

Aulagnier's psychotic material lets Lacan return to the problem of the body and the surface. The subject's access to his own body does not occur automatically. Lacan restates a radical definition: the subject is the consequence of there being a signifier and can think himself only as excluded from the signifier that determines him.

This exclusion is the opposite of personalism. The analytic subject is not the modern "person" endowed with a positive interior essence. It is what appears at the point where a field structured by signifiers cannot include the subject as one more signifier among the others.

Lacan also brings back `i(a)`, the specular image, in commenting on Aulagnier's psychotic patient before the mirror. The image remains important, but it must be situated within the signifying structure rather than treated as an independent psychological layer.

## Identification Development

The intervention shows clinically that identification can fail at the level of bodily image, phallic recognition, and the subject's position in the desire of the Other. Lacan's response radicalizes the point: identification cannot be built on a pre-existing person because the subject itself arises as excluded from the signifying field. The next step is therefore to formalize the fantasy and the object in relation to that exclusion.

# Session 19 - 9 May 1962

**Printed source pages:** 278-289

## Opening Problem

Lacan begins by correcting what he sees as the limit in Aulagnier's account of the "unsayable." Anxiety should not be located in a region outside language. The decisive fact is that there is saying and that desire is constituted through the signifying articulation of demand. This motivates another pass through topology and through the fantasy formula.

## Argument Reconstruction

### Desire is not beyond language

Demand does not stand as an obstacle to a pre-existing desire hidden behind it. The signifying articulation of demand constitutes the subject as desire. Lacan therefore rejects both a phenomenology of ineffable desire and a Hegelian picture in which a self-identical consciousness mediates between its own desire and another's.

He calls the topological route a kind of revised "transcendental aesthetic." The purpose is to escape the dominance of spherical intuition in logic. The detours through tori are not optional illustrations added after a psychological theory. They are intended to change the logical space in which the subject can be thought.

### Prohibition and desire

Lacan contrasts the hypothetical "If God does not exist, everything is permitted" with the more assertive formulation "Since God does not exist, everything is permitted." The logical form matters. Desire is not simply generated by crossing a boundary called prohibition. Law and desire determine one another in a more intimate torsion. The original knot of law and desire cannot be represented as two territories separated by a line.

### `a`, `i(a)`, and fantasy

Lacan distinguishes little `a` from the imaginary other. The latter is written `i(a)` when the emphasis is on specular form. Little `a`, by contrast, has to be grasped as the object in fantasy, and its function cannot be reduced to a biological lure.

He explicitly invokes the fantasy formula as "S barred desire of a." The formula locates fantasy as the support of desire in the field of the Other. Fantasy is where the subject responds to the question *Che vuoi?*, "What does it want?" or "What does he want?"

The subject does not simply picture an object. Fantasy gives a structure in which the barred subject and `a` are conjoined. The object emerges together with the fading or exclusion of the subject under the signifier.

### Unary identification and `-a² = 1`

A visually explicit diagram on printed page 283 places an outer field marked `-a`, an inner field marked `a`, and the overlap/interior marked `a²`. Lacan says that in fantasy the subject, formally, makes himself `-a`, the absence of `a`, before the little `a`. This is linked directly to identification with the unary trait.

He then writes the product `-a² = 1` and connects it with the mathematical symbol `√-1`. The mathematics is being used analogically but systematically: the subject's negative relation to the object and the product of the two terms return the One that the seminar has been investigating since the unary trait.

### Repetition of demand produces the object of desire

Lacan returns to the torus. The repetition of demand is a search for a unique once-only event marked by the unary trait, but each repetition can only repeat by being another occurrence. The spool-like series of demand circuits can close virtually into another loop. This additional loop depicts the object of desire.

Oral and anal objects matter analytically not because they remain need-objects but because the repetition of demand transforms them. The breast becomes an erotic object when it enters the signifying chain as the signifier of oral demand.

The factor of this transmutation is the phallic function, little `φ`. Lacan emphasizes again that the phallus is most present when absent. Its role is structural precisely because it can organize the field where the desired object is constituted through lack.

The discussion of feminine sexuality follows Freud's discovery that the phallus is demanded where it is not, namely through the mother. This impossibility of a final gift marks the path by which the phallus can become an object of desire rather than a natural organ simply waiting to be obtained.

## Identification Development

The fantasy formula joins the barred subject to the emerging object `a`, while unary identification supplies the formal One generated through the subject's negative relation to the object. Identification is therefore no longer just the repetition of a stroke. It is inserted into the structure of fantasy, where the subject fades as signifier and takes up a position relative to the object that causes the repetition of demand.

[EARLY / EMERGING OBJECT-a FORMULATION]

Here `a` is the object of desire in fantasy, constituted through the repetition of demand and correlated with the barred subject's fading. The seminar has not yet reached Seminar X's systematic account of object `a` as cause of desire in its later forms.

## Interlocutors and Sources

Aulagnier's previous intervention is the immediate point of departure. Dostoevsky's *Brothers Karamazov*, Descartes, Kant, Freud, Jones, and feminine-sexuality debates all enter the discussion. The formula of fantasy and the graph of desire are used only to the extent present in this session and are not expanded from later seminars.

## Session Pivot

The fantasy formula and `-a² = 1` connect unary identification to object `a`, but Lacan still needs a surface on which the cut itself changes the structure. Session 20 therefore develops the cross-cap and Möbius strip in detail and explicitly identifies the fantasy lozenge with a cut relation.

# Session 20 - 16 May 1962

**Printed source pages:** 290-301

## Opening Problem

Lacan justifies the increasingly technical discussion of surfaces. A surface is not an intuitive given. Rather than beginning with a ready-made three-dimensional space and placing surfaces inside it, he proposes beginning from the structure of surfaces and using them to reconstruct the notion of place. This is directly connected with the analytic "locus of the Other."

## Argument Reconstruction

### Face, edge, and surfaces without boundary

A sheet of paper seems to have two faces because it is imagined as embedded in ordinary space. Lacan asks how "face" can be defined intrinsically. He distinguishes surfaces with edges from surfaces without edges, mentioning the infinite plane, sphere, torus, and other closed surfaces.

The sphere encourages the idea that every closed surface divides an interior from an exterior. Lacan wants to break this intuition. On the torus the central hole is already more structurally important than any imagined solid interior. The torus is a surface, not a doughnut-shaped mass.

### Fundamental polygon and the cross-cap

Lacan introduces the fundamental polygon from which a surface can be reconstructed by identifying edges. The direction of the edge-arrows matters. The torus is obtained by one pattern of identifications; reversing the direction of a pair produces a different surface, represented in the source as the cross-cap or mitre.

The cross-cap drawing necessarily appears to penetrate itself when represented in ordinary three-dimensional space, but Lacan insists that the apparent line of penetration is not an edge or seam in the surface. An imagined flat being travelling on the surface can pass from what the drawing calls exterior to what it calls interior without crossing a boundary.

Inside/outside therefore fails as an intrinsic description. The self-intersection belongs to the representation in our space, not to the abstract topological surface as such.

### Signifier as cut

Lacan then asks whether the most radical essence of the signifier can be conceived as a cut in a surface. He writes elementary opposed marks such as `>` and `<` to emphasize that a signifier works through differential discontinuity.

But difference cannot be reduced to the material cut alone. The same mark, when repeated, returns as distinct because repetition places it synchronically in relation to other possible marks. The signifier can be repeated as "the same" only because inscription allows it to differ from itself in the series.

The cut matters because topology shows that a cut can change the global structure of a surface. This gives Lacan a formal model for a signifying operation whose local trace reorganizes the whole field.

### Möbius strip and non-orientability

The Möbius strip is introduced as the simplest illustration of the one-sided property needed for the cross-cap. A strip is given a half-twist and its ends joined. A line or oriented circle carried along the surface returns with its ordinary left/right orientation transformed relative to an external observer.

Lacan calls such surfaces non-orientable, but he immediately plays on the paradox that the object can appear more rigidly "oriented" in another sense: turning it over does not produce a distinguishable reverse side. There is no stable pair of faces.

### The decisive cut

If the Möbius strip is cut along its middle line, the cut returns to its starting point. The result remains a single connected strip, but the structure has changed: the new strip is orientable and has two sides. A single cut has therefore transformed a global property of every point of the surface.

This is exactly why cut is useful for psychoanalysis. A signifying operation cannot be thought merely as a local mark laid onto an otherwise unchanged substance. It can change the structure of the field in which the subject is located.

### The fantasy lozenge as cut

Lacan now returns to the quadrilateral/lozenge `◊` in the fantasy formula `$ ◊ a`. He says he has never adequately verbalized this shape. In the present context he treats the barred subject in fantasy as, properly speaking, the cut of `a`.

The question becomes: how can the field of desire, isolated from demand in its ungraspable aspect, be knotted through a torsion to the field of object `a`? This is the topological problem that will dominate the remaining sessions.

## Identification Development

The unary trait is recast through the cut. A signifier is a differential inscription that repeats as another occurrence, and a cut can alter an entire surface without adding a new substance. Identification can therefore be understood as a structural effect of inscription and cutting rather than the attachment of a positive property to an already completed self.

## Interlocutors and Sources

The principal interlocutor is mathematical topology. Traditional anatomy is invoked critically because it treats bodily orifices as already given rather than as signifying cuts. Freud and Fenichel appear in relation to oral identification and bodily zones. The source notes that this week's text is reconstructed from notes and that Hooson follows a discursive version where the surviving records diverge.

[TRANSLATOR NOTE - BEN HOOSON]

Hooson reports that no stenotype survives for 16 May 1962. The Rue Claude Bernard version is itself marked as based on notes, and Roussan also gives a discursive version drawing especially on notes by Jean Laplanche and Jean Oury. Hooson mainly follows that discursive version and records significant differences in footnotes. This is a genuine source-level uncertainty for the session.

## Session Pivot

The cut has become the bridge between signifier and topology, and `$ ◊ a` has been tied explicitly to that bridge. The next block follows the consequences through the cross-cap, fantasy, desire, and the extraction of object `a` from a surface whose structure changes under cutting.

# Session 21 - 23 May 1962

**Printed source pages:** 302-315

## Opening Problem

Lacan asks whether a signifier can "grasp" the slightest thing. Classical logic, organized around universal predication and the *dictum de omni et nullo*, tends to treat the objects it captures as if they could be enclosed in a class and, in principle, reduced to nullity. Lacan returns to Euler circles in order to show why this model is inadequate for the object of desire and for the subject produced by a cut.

## Argument Reconstruction

### Universal predication and nullifiability

An ordinary Euler circle on a plane is reducible: one can contract it until its enclosed field vanishes. This gives a visual support to the universal proposition. A class may even be empty without invalidating the universal statement. Lacan uses examples about teachers and psychoanalysts to distinguish universal predication from existential definition. "All psychoanalysts have been analysed" cannot simply be represented by putting one class-circle inside another and assuming that existence has thereby been established.

The forgotten problem is desire. Logic developed by trying to seize and keep an object, and *Begriff* itself carries the etymological resonance of grasping. But the object of desire is structurally elusive. The effort to possess it cannot be separated from the logical forms used to define objects.

### From line to cut

Lacan returns to the closed line. On a plane or sphere a simple closed curve usually divides the surface into two pieces. On a torus the same visual line can have a radically different effect. A loop can remain a cut without separating the surface.

The Möbius strip makes the point sharper. A median cut changes the topology of the strip without splitting it into two independent pieces. The resulting object is no longer a Möbius strip. This shows that the cut is not a passive border. It can generate a new structural organization.

### Cut as generator of surfaces

Lacan therefore reverses the intuitive order. Rather than saying that a pre-existing surface permits certain cuts, he explores how surfaces can be generated and classified from the possibilities of a cut. The sphere, torus, and cross-cap are treated as organizations of holes and edge-identifications.

In the torus, a cut can be stretched and its edges joined to produce the corridor or handle that makes the toroidal hole. The hole is not a hidden volume. It is a structural consequence of how the surface is cut and rejoined.

### Position of object `a`

At the point where a cut organizes an irreducible hole, Lacan places object `a`. The object is not a positive little thing lodged inside a psychic cavity. It is situated by the operation that makes the hole count. The torus offered one version of this structure, but the cross-cap now promises a more exact relation among cut, point, object, and phallus.

The cross-cap includes a privileged point at the termination of the apparent self-penetration line. The apparent crossing is not a true seam in the surface. Lacan progressively isolates this point as the place around which the topology of the surface is organized.

The phallus is assigned the operator-function that allows an object `a` to be placed where a lack is structurally produced. The point is not yet fully worked out, but Lacan is clearly moving from a general topology of lack to a specific topology of fantasy.

### Interior eight and the recutting of a cut

The "interior eight" returns as the minimal form in which a cut can recross its own path. The crossing point is not treated as a mere accident of drawing. It becomes a candidate for formalizing the privileged point of the cross-cap.

A cut on a torus can wind repeatedly without closing in the same way. On one-sided surfaces, by contrast, the number and manner of turns can transform the topology of the resulting strip. Lacan uses these differences to isolate the relation between the subject's cut and the object that emerges from it.

## Identification Development

Identification with the unary trait is now inseparable from the cut that produces a hole. The signifier does not grasp an already existing identity. It institutes a field by cutting it, and the object appears at the point where the cut cannot be absorbed into a universal class. Identification thus moves from "one mark" to the structural consequences of the mark on the surface of the subject.

## Interlocutors and Sources

Classical logic and Euler diagrams are the main formal background. Lacan also alludes to the history of *Begriff* as grasping and to the analytic relation to object-possession. The topology of sphere, torus, Möbius strip, and cross-cap becomes the principal technical language.

## Session Pivot

The cut has become generative rather than merely divisive, and object `a` has been placed at the irreducible hole produced by that operation. Session 22 makes the reversal explicit: the cut engenders the surface, and the double cut on the projective plane becomes the model for the fantasy relation `$ ◊ a`.

# Session 22 - 30 May 1962

**Printed source pages:** 316-331

## Opening Problem

Lacan defends the topological detours as consequences of analytic experience. If the subject is an effect of the signifier, then the most abstract fields, including mathematics, must eventually be reconsidered from that premise. He briefly invokes transfinite number and bi-univocal correspondence, then returns to the unary trait and to the cut.

## Argument Reconstruction

### Counting before number

The theory of transfinite numbers is used to recall a primitive relation prior to constituted number: one-to-one correspondence, stroke for stroke. This is exactly the field in which the unary trait has been situated. Counting depends on a prior possibility of pairing marks, and the subject appears in the operation rather than as a completed entity that subsequently counts.

### The signifier is a cut

Lacan states the year's thesis in compact form: the signifier is a cut, and the subject and its structure must be made to depend on this cut. The Möbius strip has shown that a median cut can transform the very type of surface. Hence it is legitimate to invert the everyday picture and say that the cut can engender the surface.

He distances this from a crude anthropology of "man the cutting animal." Castration gives the clinical background, but the analytic cut is first of all a signifying discontinuity. A line may itself be treated as an original cut, each of its points or elements being a section of that cut.

### The interior eight as a cut that cuts itself

The interior eight condenses this operation. A closed curve is not closed because a subject knows in advance that it will return to its origin. Closure is supplied by the real encounter with its own trace. "Only the real closes the cut." The cut proper is therefore a stroke that cuts itself.

This gives the crossing point a privileged status. The point is generated through the cut's recrossing of its own place, not through the coincidence of two independent lines.

### Single and double cuts on the projective plane

Lacan now analyzes the cross-cap/projective plane. A simple cut that avoids the privileged point can open the surface without dividing it. A cut that passes in a particular way through or around the point-hole produces a Möbius band as the remaining one-sided surface.

The point-hole cannot simply be abolished. Even when reduced to something punctiform it plays the role of an edge or hole necessary to preserve the topology. A Möbius band has one edge, and a cross-cap can be understood as organizing that edge in a more complex closed-surface form.

A double-circuit cut is the first cut that divides the projective plane in the relevant way. It separates two components: a Möbius surface and a "central piece." The central piece carries the distinctive cross-cap structure, including the self-crossing representation ending at the point-hole.

### `$ ◊ a` as subject cut of object

This division gives Lacan the schematic relation he could not obtain from the torus alone. He repeatedly describes the fantasy as "$ cut of a." The barred subject and object `a` are two terms linked by the function of the cut.

The Möbius remainder and central piece are not declared literally identical with `$` and `a` in a naive one-to-one way. Rather, their relation supplies a structural support for fantasy: a one-sided subject-surface is separated from an object-piece by a cut that itself depends on a privileged point.

The unary trait now reappears within this topology. The subject marked by the unary stroke has an indirect relation to what is hidden behind specular identification. Fantasy formalizes that relation to the object where the Other lacks a universal witness or guarantee.

### Phallus, psychosis, and desire

The big phallus `Φ` is assigned to the privileged point that gives consistency to the central piece. Lacan contrasts this with psychotic organization, where the subject's own body can occupy an overwhelming position in the structure of desire.

He also brings in Sade to approach the impossible point of desire. Human desire is "acosmic" in the sense that it cannot be harmonized with a natural order that would assign each object its proper place. The impossible is not an accidental obstacle placed in the way of desire; it is one of the points from which desire receives its structure.

## Identification Development

The unary mark is now explicitly articulated with the cut of fantasy. Identification creates neither a transparent self nor a stable mirror identity. The subject is the one-sided remainder produced by a cut that also isolates an object-function. The One of the unary trait and the object of desire are therefore linked through a structural division rather than through complementarity.

## Interlocutors and Sources

Cantorian/transfinite mathematics is invoked briefly through one-to-one correspondence. Castration gives the clinical horizon of the cut. Sade appears as a reference for the impossible in desire. The main evidence is the topology of Möbius strip and projective plane.

## Session Pivot

Session 22 produces the decisive schema: a double cut on the projective plane isolates a Möbius remainder and central object-piece, allowing Lacan to formalize fantasy as `$ cut of a`. Session 23 returns to the torus to compare subject and Other, then reapplies the interior-eight cut to the cross-cap in a more exact analysis of the privileged point.

# Session 23 - 6 June 1962

**Printed source pages:** 332-354

## Opening Problem

Lacan resumes with the "signifier of the cut," also called the interior eight, loop, or "Polish signifier." He wants a name that draws attention to its purely signifying function rather than to a visual resemblance. A surface, in the sense relevant here, is organized around such a cut.

## Argument Reconstruction

### The torus reconstructed from edge-identification

Lacan recalls the torus as generated from a quadrilateral fundamental polygon whose edges are identified in oriented pairs. The familiar toroidal figure is secondary. The relations of edge correspondence define the surface.

On the torus, repeated reel-like demand circuits go around the constitutive void. Their repetition draws another contour, the circle around the central hole, which has served as the place of the object of desire. A third oblique circuit can combine the two functions. In the source figures Lacan marks a demand circuit `D`, an object circle `a`, and an oblique desire-cut `d`.

The torus is useful precisely because it shows the difficulty of ordering desire and object. The place of `a` is initially only the place of a nothing. The torus does not itself determine which particular object will occupy it.

### Chained tori and "desire of the Other"

Lacan then returns to two chained tori, one representing the subject `$`, the other the Other `A`. A privileged oblique circle on one can be transferred to the other. After taking account of the ninety-degree relation of the linked tori, the circles can be superimposed. The construction is used to image the formula that the desire of the subject is the desire of the Other.

But if the loop winds in a more complicated ratio, the superposition fails. Lacan uses this to formalize the neurotic cross-equivalence: the subject's demand is related to the object of the Other, while the subject's object is related to the demand of the Other. The identity of the two desires is thereby shown as an impasse rather than a fusion.

### From torus to cross-cap and fantasy

The torus cannot finally formalize fantasy, so Lacan returns to the projective plane. The cross-cap promises a surface on which the double cut can carry the central organizing function of desire.

He spends part of the session clarifying the construction of the projective plane from a circular edge whose points are identified antipodally. No metric distance is decisive. What matters is relative position and the point-by-point correspondence of the edge.

### The privileged origin-point

Because antipodal identification gives no naturally privileged starting point, Lacan introduces an *archē*-point, an origin that has a special structural function. He connects this with the interior loop of the interior-eight cut. Applied to the cross-cap, the cut goes twice around the privileged point.

This is not a decorative central dot. The double circuit has a unique cutting property. A simple cut can open the projective plane without dividing it, but a cut going twice around the privileged point divides the surface. A third circuit does not simply repeat the same effect. The two-turn cut is structurally exceptional.

### Dissymmetry and the isolated piece

The component isolated by the double cut is left/right dissymmetric. Turning it over does not produce an object superimposable on its mirror image. Lacan compares this with handedness and the spiral of a shell. This dissymmetry is important because he has been seeking a way to distinguish functions that the torus by itself left reversible.

The remaining surface is Möbius-like, while the isolated central piece carries the point-hole and the special cross-cap structure. These two complementary products of the cut will support the barred subject and object relation in fantasy.

## Identification Development

The subject's relation to the Other is no longer represented as simple matching. The torus shows crossed demand/object relations, while the projective plane provides the dissymmetry required for fantasy. Identification with the unary trait remains on the side of a subject that repeats through a cut, but the object gains a topologically distinct consistency through the double circuit around the privileged point.

# Session 24 - 13 June 1962

**Printed source pages:** 355-374

## Opening Problem

Lacan starts immediately with three numbered figures. Hooson explicitly warns that the correlation between text and topological diagrams in this seminar is particularly difficult and that Roussan's own explanatory appendix does not fully resolve every point. This session therefore requires the strongest fail-forward discipline in the reconstruction.

## Argument Reconstruction

### Opening the projective plane

Figure 1 shows a simple cut of the projective plane/cross-cap. Such a cut opens the surface without immediately dividing it. Figure 2 is an opened-out representation intended to make the privileged point and the apparently crossing sheets more intelligible. Figure 3 gives an intermediate deformation.

Lacan repeatedly insists on the difference between the intrinsic surface and its extrinsic rendering in three-dimensional space. The line where two sheets appear to penetrate one another is not an actual seam. Once the surface is cut, the sheets can be pulled apart in the drawing because their apparent coincidence in ordinary space has no intrinsic topological significance.

### The point-hole

The terminal point of the pseudo-penetration line becomes the central object of the session. Lacan treats it as a "point-hole": it looks punctiform but performs the function of a hole or edge in the organization of the surface.

The point cannot be suppressed without changing the surface. If the projective plane is cut through the point in the wrong way, the result reduces to a Möbius band. Even when the remaining hole is arbitrarily small, it is topologically indispensable because it stands in for the single edge required by the Möbius structure.

The point-hole is therefore a paradoxical concentration of an edge into a point. It organizes the one-sidedness of the projective plane while resisting representation as an ordinary point of Euclidean space.

### Figures 4-6 and the central piece

Lacan progressively isolates the central piece created by the double cut. In Figure 4 the rest of the cross-cap is mentally erased, leaving a plane that crosses itself along a finite line ending at a point. Figure 5 shifts the point and clarifies how the edges must be paired. Figure 6 gives a simplified edge-identification in which opposite orientations are glued to one another.

These constructions expose the Möbius logic hidden inside the projective plane. The cut that produces the central piece also leaves a one-sided remainder. The two parts are not mirror copies. One preserves the one-sided Möbius property, while the central piece carries the special point-hole and the distinctive dissymmetry of the cross-cap.

### Double cut as the first divisive cut

A single circuit can open the projective plane without splitting it. The double-circuit cut is the minimal operation that divides it. This is the technical reason Lacan has given the interior eight such importance. Its two lobes and its self-relation are not a pictorial metaphor pasted onto fantasy after the fact. The cut has exactly the kind of divisive yet structure-preserving effect required to formalize the barred subject and object.

### Fantasy as `$ cut of a`

Lacan again says that the double cut gives a schematic representation of `$ cut of a`, the fantasy structure `$ ◊ a`. The subject and object are two terms, but the cut is constitutive of both. The barred subject is not one piece of a previously whole subject, and `a` is not the complementary piece that would restore wholeness.

The unary trait supports the subject's mark, while the point-hole and central piece give object `a` a structural place in relation to the lack of the Other. This is the seminar's most advanced formulation so far of the object as produced through the cut rather than recovered as a lost natural object.

### Phallus and the privileged point

The big phallus `Φ` is again identified with the point that gives consistency to the central piece. The phallus has a double function: it appears at the level of the barred subject and authenticates the object for desire. This is why it cannot simply be identified with an organ.

Lacan then returns to clinical and philosophical material, including Sade, Plato, Socrates, and Alcibiades. The object sought in the beloved is not simply a set of attractive properties. Alcibiades wants to see Socrates desire, to locate the desirer in the heart of the privileged object. The phallic function becomes the mediator of this radical implication of the subject in the desired object.

The formulation remains paradoxical: one can be the phallus for another without anyone being able to state whose phallus one finally is. The point is not an identity but a structural place in the desire of the Other.

## Identification Development

Identification is now integrated with the topology of fantasy. The unary trait marks the subject, but the marked subject exists only through a cut that also isolates object `a`. The phallus occupies the privileged point that gives the object-piece consistency. Identification therefore cannot be understood independently of fantasy, lack in the Other, and the object around which desire is organized.

[EARLY / EMERGING OBJECT-a FORMULATION]

Object `a` is here materially supported by the central piece isolated from the projective plane and by the point-hole that organizes it. This is a historically specific Seminar IX construction and should not be silently replaced by the later list of breast, faeces, gaze, and voice as standardized forms of object `a`.

## Interlocutors and Sources

Roussan's graphics are indispensable to this session and Hooson's notes repeatedly flag topological ambiguity. [TRANSLATOR NOTE - BEN HOOSON]

Hooson states that more work is needed to clarify exactly what Lacan means in some of the explanations attached to the 13 June figures. He notes that Roussan supplies extensive topological notes but that he himself cannot fully understand all of Roussan's explanations. This uncertainty is retained rather than resolved externally.

## Session Pivot

By 13 June the seminar has a mature topological schema: the double cut divides the projective plane into a Möbius remainder and a central piece organized by a point-hole, giving structural support to `$ ◊ a`. The final two sessions use this result to draw the threads of identification, fantasy, object, phallus, and desire together.

# Session 25 - 20 June 1962

**Printed source pages:** 375-388

## Opening Problem

With the year ending, Lacan takes stock of the seminar's path through Freud's forms of identification. He says he began from Freud's second form, identification by a single trait, and has tried to make it impossible to think this henceforth except through the unary stroke. The later topological work with the interior eight has moved him into the field of Freud's third identification, where the subject is constituted as desire in relation to the desire of the Other.

## Argument Reconstruction

### Reassembling Freud's identifications

Lacan distinguishes rather than collapses Freud's forms. Identification with the father remains the most mysterious and historically expansive. To have made it the seminar's starting point would have required a sustained treatment of *Totem and Taboo*, which Lacan deliberately did not undertake.

The second identification, via the *einziger Zug*, has supplied the main formal tool: the unary trait. Freud's third identification, especially visible in hysteria, has become the route by which the subject is constituted as desire through the locus of the Other. Freud's work on group psychology also shows that the object and ego ideal can converge around the unique leader, giving a concrete point where the forms of identification touch one another without becoming one taxonomy.

### A logic of desire and object

Lacan invokes Lévi-Strauss's *Totemism* and *The Savage Mind*, both recent in 1962, as evidence of the radical signifying organization of classificatory systems. Structural anthropology, however, cannot replace psychoanalytic logic. The latter must account for the object of desire and the point at which classification is disrupted by lack.

The point `Φ` introduced through the cross-cap is now described as participating not merely in the mediation but in the constitution of the barred subject and little `a` in fantasy. The subject is "the cut of this object." The relation is as intimate as front and back on a one-sided surface, not as two detachable pieces of an original whole.

Lacan links this to Freud's *Urverdrängung*, primal repression, and to the dream's "navel," the point where interpretation encounters the unknown. Desire has a structural navel that cannot be abolished by producing more meanings.

### Neurotic, perverse, psychotic: three normal terms, not three complete worlds

Lacan warns against rushing from the formal construction to a catalogue of clinical types. He provocatively says that the psychotic is "normal" in psychosis, the pervert in perversion, and the neurotic in neurosis, because body, phallus, and big Other are all normal terms in the constitution of desire. The structures differ in how these terms are organized and misrecognized, not because one structure possesses desire and another lacks it.

The psychotic is especially tied to the body, the pervert to the phallic function, and the neurotic to the Other. These are not diagnostic slogans intended to replace clinical work. They are reminders that the same structural terms are present across configurations.

### Body and drive are not biologism

Lacan strongly rejects the interpretation of Freud's drives as crude biological theory. The drive's relation to the body is topological: inside/outside, route, edge, and return are more decisive than any newly discovered physiology. Psychoanalysis has not yielded new biological organs or sensory mechanisms. Its body is a body structured by signifying cuts.

This also bears on the aim of analysis. Adaptation to ordinary duties can occur, but Lacan treats such adaptation as at most a secondary outcome. The serious question is when and how an analysis allows a subject to enter the field of his desire. For analysts, this becomes the question of the analyst's desire and of how an analyst can occupy a position that does not simply restore conventional identification.

### Mystical comparison and the object

Lacan briefly uses Muslim and Hindu mystical terminology, especially via Louis Massignon, to note traditions in which a subject is progressively concentrated into or through an object. He does not identify mystical realization with analysis. The comparison serves to show that an object can function as a turning point in the subject's relation to desire.

He relates this to `$ ◊ a`: the subject assumes a relation to an object that is neither a simple possession nor a mirror counterpart.

### Wolf Man, number, and the non-specular object

The Wolf Man's fantasy provides a vivid object-field. Lacan notes the discrepancy between the number of wolves in the drawing and in Freud's text. The exact count is less important than the fact that the object of desire carries number. It is numerical in a way linked to splitting, repetition, and the unary mark.

The object appearing in fantasy carries the splits of the subject. Lacan describes the double loop as a radical repetition: it makes the circuit twice and thereby gives temporality to the topological space of desire.

This allows him to return polemically to formal logic. Its principle `a = a` rests on identity, but the signifier as such is different from itself. Nothing of the subject can identify with a signifier without at the same time being excluded from it. That self-difference opens the logical place at which the object can be constituted.

Human beings "take their desires for realities" because reality itself is constituted along the channel furrowed by desire. The statement is not an excuse for fantasy replacing reality. It is a claim about the structural conditions under which a world of objects can appear for a speaking subject.

## Identification Development

The session explicitly gathers the seminar's trajectory. Freud's single-trait identification has become the unary stroke; Freud's hysterical identification has become the subject's constitution as desire through the Other; and paternal identification remains the unresolved historical edge. The topology of fantasy joins these developments by making the subject the cut of an object rather than the bearer of a stable identity.

## Interlocutors and Sources

Freud is central through *Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego*, *Totem and Taboo*, primal repression, the dream's navel, and the Wolf Man. Hegel appears through *die Sache selbst*. Lévi-Strauss supplies structural classification. Louis Massignon and mystical terminology are comparative references. Serge Leclaire's work on fantasy is discussed as evidence of how Lacan's students were using the year's tools.

## Session Pivot

Session 25 gathers the unary trait, fantasy, topology, number, and object into one logic of desire. The final session shifts the accent decisively onto little `a` as the object of castration and asks what kind of object psychoanalysis itself has discovered.

# Session 26 - 27 June 1962

**Printed source pages:** 389-406

## Opening Problem

Lacan chooses the formula supporting Freud's third identification as his final axis. The source renders it verbally as the barred subject read through a "cut of little a," the relation elsewhere written `$ ◊ a`. He explicitly declines to make the phallic point `φ` or `Φ` the final stopping place. Instead he puts the accent on little `a`, both as the object structuring psychic reality and as the object specific to analytic science.

## Argument Reconstruction

### Object of castration

Lacan proposes a logical distinction among objects of privation, frustration, and castration. The worldly object classified by attributes can be treated as an object of privation: one may possess or fail to possess the defining trait. The object of frustration is organized through demand and the refusal or failure of a gift. The analytic object Lacan wants to isolate is different: it is the object of castration.

The distinction takes him back to Aristotelian logic. Aristotle's object is defined by attributes that can belong to it and by classes constituted through these predicates. This logic confuses, or at least overlays, being and having. The unary trait is central because class-membership turns on possession or non-possession of a characteristic trait.

Lévi-Strauss's classificatory oppositions are invoked as a contrasting logic of paired differences, closer in some respects to Platonic division. Lacan's concern is not to adjudicate the history of logic but to recover the cut that made the Aristotelian object possible and then show what analytic experience forces us to add.

### "All that glitters is not gold"

The proverb lets Lacan expose the limits of a simple Euler-circle reading of negation. Its meaning is not exhausted by placing some glittering things inside the class of gold and others outside it. What is put in question is "goldness" itself, the quality that would guarantee the object's fascinating brilliance.

Gold therefore becomes a figure for what gives an object the color of desire. No positive gold can finally guarantee the point around which desire turns. Little `a` is this object put radically in question, not the final authenticated member of a class.

### The double cut and the extraction of `a`

Lacan returns to the cross-cap. The double cut can be enlarged and displaced while preserving its topology. When the relevant piece is extracted, what remains is a Möbius surface. The removal of the object reorganizes the entire remainder.

This gives a concrete meaning to the object of castration. `a` is not merely what is missing from a pre-existing world. Its extraction is constitutive of the world's organization. Lacan compares the operation to cutting a seal or stamp from a surface: what is removed and the trace left behind belong to the same operation.

At the point where the signifying power of the Other fails, and where the phallic point marks the abolition of any final guarantee of meaning, little `a` takes its place.

### From cross-cap to world

Lacan restates the cross-cap construction as a sphere with a hole organized by antipodal identifications. Extracting the object-piece leaves the rest transformed into a Möbius surface. He calls this an "enucleation" of the object of castration. The world is then ordered in a certain fashion and can present the illusion of coherent worldhood.

Against the Aristotelian object and against the tempting natural-object model of *Naturwissenschaft*, Lacan inserts the analytic object. Goethe's morphology and quasi-cosmological reading of nature serve as the contrasting temptation to see meaningful forms everywhere in nature. Psychoanalytic objecthood arises instead through desire and loss.

Goethe's abandonment of Friederike is used as a biographical example of how renunciation of a desired object can organize a world. Lacan links the structure to his earlier discussion of individual myth and the Rat Man.

### `a`, `i(a)`, and cause

The object of constitutive castration, `a`, has a complementary relation to what remains and especially to the specular figure `i(a)`. In the fundamental mirror misrecognition, the barred subject can take the function of specular image, but the image is not the representation of `a` and is not its complement.

Lacan provocatively reintroduces the word "cause." The barred subject could be the cause of `i(a)`, and cause itself should be sought where effects are cut out rather than in a hidden positive entity behind them.

The partial object likewise cannot be reduced to a fragment of a once-whole body. It designates the point at which loss and repression are organized.

### The acosmic point of desire

The object of castration designates an acosmic point around which the apparently objectal world is constituted. It emerges at the failure of the Other, at the loss of a signifier, and Lacan compares it to the unrecovered member in the myth of Horus/Osiris.

Because the subject is essentially the cut of this object, a gap can arise between perception and consciousness. Lacan links this to self-consciousness and to the ancient formula discussed by Heidegger from Parmenides, "thinking and being are the same." He rejects the interpretation that simply identifies being with cognition. In his construction, barred subject and little `a` lie on the same side of a dyadic structure opposed to the image of a completed world.

Little `a` is what is missing from the text of the world. The return of the repressed circulates around that missing object rather than restoring it.

### The image masks access to the object

The mirror image `i(a)` envelops access to the object of castration. The image is itself an object, but not object `a` and not a representative that transparently depicts it. The source develops several optical and specular comparisons to show how image and object can mask each other.

Lacan returns to the fantasy: `$ ◊ a` is analogous, at the level of desire, to the relation of the ego to the specular image. Yet the two relations are not identical. The desirer is sought at the heart of the object, in response to *Che vuoi?*.

The hysteric gives the clearest Freudian example. She identifies not simply with another person but with the desire of the Other, and her symptoms and affects can appear as conventional or mimetic inscriptions where that desire leaves its trace.

### Frustration, envelopes, and the father

In the final pages Lacan returns to frustration and the body. The primitive relation should not be imagined simply as a total mother-child unity later deprived of satisfaction. He points instead to bodily envelopes and membranes, structures in which inside and outside have a more complex continuity.

Incorporation also has to be reconsidered on the side of the father, a dimension he acknowledges having left largely untreated because it would require the religious and historical field associated with paternal identification.

The child asks the mother for what she does not have, the phallus. Analytic theories that treat mother-child gratification as a closed dyad therefore miss the structural divergence built into demand.

Lacan ends by returning to Freud's unfinished work on splitting of the ego. The object of castration is so ambiguous that when the subject represses it, he can establish it more firmly in the Other. Psychoanalysis will remain theoretically and institutionally unsettled until it recognizes this object as its own object of science, just as number or quantity can function as objects for mathematics.

He announces that the following year's seminar will take up anxiety from this point.

## Identification Development

The seminar closes by defining identification through a structural triad: unary mark, cut subject, and object of castration. Freud's third identification is formalized not as copying another person but as the subject's constitution through the desire of the Other. The subject is the cut of `a`, while `i(a)` gives a specular mask that must not be confused with the object. Identification therefore ends not in identity but in a logic of difference, loss, fantasy, and desire.

[EARLY / EMERGING OBJECT-a FORMULATION]

The final Seminar IX formulation treats little `a` as the object of castration, the object missing from the text of the world, structurally extracted by the double cut and correlated with the failure of the Other. This anticipates but is not identical with the more systematic object-cause theory of Seminar X.

## Interlocutors and Sources

Aristotle supplies the formal logic of attribute and class; Plato and Parmenides enter the historical-logical discussion; Heidegger is cited in connection with the pre-Socratic formula. Lévi-Strauss remains a reference for classificatory thought. Goethe and Theodor Reik appear in the discussion of object-renunciation and world-formation. Freud is decisive throughout: hysteria, the desire of the Other, inhibition/symptom/anxiety, frustration, the Wolf Man's veil, incorporation, castration, and the splitting of the ego.

[TRANSLATOR NOTE - BEN HOOSON]

At the opening Hooson records a genuine textual ambiguity over what Lacan said in glossing the formula: Typescript 1, Rue Claude Bernard, and Roussan differ. Hooson prefers Roussan's "cut of little a" because it best fits the argument that follows. This reconstruction retains that reading while marking the source uncertainty.

## Session Pivot

The final session does not close identification into a complete system. It leaves paternal identification and the full theory of anxiety open. What it does establish is a rigorous trajectory from the unary trait to the subject as cut, from demand to desire, and from lack to an emerging object `a` that is structurally produced rather than naturally given.

# 2. Identification Conceptual Trajectory

The seminar begins by refusing to treat identification as a simple relation of resemblance. Freud's distinctions are retained, but Lacan works through them chronologically rather than imposing a finished taxonomy from the outset.

The decisive early move is from identity to difference. A signifier is not self-identical in the way classical logic writes `a = a`; it exists by differential relation to other signifiers. Freud's *einziger Zug* therefore becomes the unary trait, the minimal stroke by which an occurrence is marked as one precisely because it differs from every other occurrence.

From the unary trait Lacan passes to writing, the proper name, counting, and repetition. Repetition is never the return of an identical substance. The repeated mark is "the same" only as another inscription. The subject appears in the interval opened by that repetition and increasingly acquires the status of a missing or subtractive term.

The torus then gives this structure spatial form. Repeated demand-circuits generate another circuit not separately counted by the subject. Desire emerges from the repetitive field of demand without becoming one more demand. The subject's relation to the Other is represented by crossed toroidal circuits in which demand and desire fail to coincide.

As the seminar advances, the torus proves insufficient because it does not intrinsically supply the needed asymmetry. The cross-cap/projective plane, Möbius strip, and interior-eight cut allow Lacan to formalize one-sidedness, the failure of ordinary inside/outside, and a cut that transforms the entire surface.

Fantasy becomes the privileged structure. `$ ◊ a` is repeatedly verbalized as the barred subject as "cut of a." The object does not complete the subject. It is structurally isolated through the same cut by which the subject is constituted.

The last sessions return to Freud. The second identification has been reconstructed through the unary trait. The third, especially hysterical identification through the desire of the Other, is reconstructed through fantasy and object. The first, identification with the father, is explicitly left only partly treated because it would require the historical, religious, and paternal field of *Totem and Taboo*.

# 3. Unary Trait / One / Repetition Map

- **Sessions 1-3:** Lacan dismantles self-sameness and shows that the One relevant to the signifier is a mark of difference.
- **Sessions 4-6:** tally marks, writing, and proper names make the unary function visible as inscription rather than resemblance.
- **Sessions 7-9:** the One is linked with recursive notation, negative determination, object-function, and `√-1`.
- **Sessions 10-11:** `Einheit` is distinguished from *Einzigkeit*; Freud's *einziger Zug* is the singular trait rather than an integrating unity.
- **Session 12:** repeated demand-circuits on the torus produce an additional circuit that the subject does not count, giving topological support to the constitutive minus-one.
- **Sessions 15-17:** repetition is represented by toroidal circuits and the inverted eight; the "same" loop returns only through structural difference.
- **Session 19:** unary identification is joined to the fantasy relation; `-a² = 1` and `√-1` connect the negative subject/object relation with the One.
- **Sessions 20-24:** the unary mark becomes a cut whose repetition/recutting changes a surface and produces the point-hole and object-piece.
- **Sessions 25-26:** Lacan explicitly returns to Freud's second identification and states that it must now be understood through the unary stroke; formal identity `a = a` is criticized because the signifier is different from itself.

# 4. Proper Name / Letter / Writing Map

The proper-name sequence is concentrated in the first third of the seminar but remains foundational for the later topology.

- **Session 4:** writing and tally marks show that a mark can persist independently of resemblance to what it marks.
- **Session 6:** Lacan contrasts Bertrand Russell's treatment of the proper name with Gardiner's account and turns to ancient writing, hieroglyphs, and Champollion. The proper name is bound to the letter and to transmissible inscription rather than to a bundle of descriptive qualities.
- **Session 7:** names of letters and recursive notation further separate inscription from meaning. A name can function as a mark in a chain even when it does not transparently signify the subject it names.
- **Sessions 8-11:** logical notation and unary marks extend the same principle: writing makes difference countable and permits a subject to be represented without being made present as a substance.
- **Sessions 20-26:** topology radicalizes the earlier writing thesis. The signifier is a cut in a surface, and the line of inscription can transform the global structure. Letter, stroke, and cut become successive formalizations of the same problem of how a mark produces rather than merely records difference.

# End of Seminar IX Reconstruction

This file reconstructs the complete supplied Ben Hooson English translation of Jacques Lacan's Seminar IX, *Identification* (1961-1962).

Processing mode:

Mode B - exhaustive structured reconstruction.

The file preserves all 26 supplied sessions and treats topological figures selectively but substantively.

## Reconstruction Integrity Notes

- The source itself contains numerous translator notes recording disagreement among Typescript 1, the Rue Claude Bernard version, Michel Roussan's critical version, and listener notes. This reconstruction follows Hooson's supplied decisions and does not resolve them externally.
- Session 20 (16 May 1962) has no surviving stenotype in Hooson's account; the supplied text is reconstructed from note-based versions. Several exact phrasings therefore remain source-level uncertainties.
- Hooson explicitly says that the correlation between text and diagrams in the first half of Session 24 (13 June 1962) is particularly puzzling. Several edge orientations and pseudo-crossings are therefore marked as partially unclear rather than reconstructed beyond the source.
- Cross-cap drawings necessarily show apparent self-intersections when represented in ordinary three-dimensional space. The reconstruction consistently treats these as extrinsic drawing devices, not literal seams in the abstract surface.
- Several small arrowheads, edge labels, and orientation marks in the topological figures are difficult to read. Where the local operation is clear but exact orientation is not, the file uses `[TOPOLOGICAL ORIENTATION UNCLEAR IN SOURCE]` or equivalent uncertainty language.
- The fantasy operator is visually and textually represented with some extraction inconsistency. The reconstruction uses `$ ◊ a` because the supplied source later explicitly identifies the quadrilateral/lozenge and verbalizes the relation as `$ cut of a`; local extraction that resembles an arrow is treated as a source/rendering ambiguity rather than a different formula.
- Small `φ` and capital `Φ` are not always typographically stable in extracted text. The reconstruction preserves the local phallic-point function and flags symbol uncertainty where necessary.
- No session was supplemented from another translation, another Lacan seminar, secondary commentary, or external chronology.
